narrative: During the 1950s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and identity. While specific details about this decade are limited in our source material, we can infer that hairstyles such as cornrows, a style of three-strand braids close to the scalp, were likely prevalent among African cultures and their diaspora communities. The afro, created by combing out natural growth or using chemical curling products, would have also been a prominent hairstyle during this time. As for protective hairstyles, which aim to reduce hair breakage and exposure to environmental elements, box braids and locs (dreadlocks) may have emerged as popular options among Black women seeking to preserve their natural textures. Unfortunately, our source material does not provide more detailed insights into the specific hairstyles and hair practices of this era, but it is clear that African cultures placed great importance on traditional hairstyles as a means of self-expression, identity, and community connection.
